--- layout: dilemma permalink: /dilemmas/utilitarian-ethics-tortured-child/ title: "The Tortured Child" summary: "You can build a perfectly happy society, but it requires the endless torture of one child." ---

Suppose you were called upon to rebuild human society so that everyone in the world would be happy and would find peace and tranquility. There is a way to do this, but you know that it requires the ongoing torture of a child.

The child must be locked in a small outhouse somewhere and remain in torture and desperation. However, through the misery and tears of this one child, you can build a society where everyone else is happy.

Would you agree to set up society this way?

Source: Ursula K. Le Guin, "The Ones Who Walk Away from Omelas" (1973), first published in New Dimensions 3 and collected in The Wind's Twelve Quarters

PDF of the story

See also: Ursula K. Le Guin, Fyodor Dostoevsky, and the Comfort of Cruelty, Gizmodo — on the connection between the two stories

See also: Fyodor Dostoyevsky, The Brothers Karamazov ("Imagine that you are creating a fabric of human destiny...")

See also: William James, "The Moral Philosopher and the Moral Life" (1891), in The Will to Believe — "millions kept permanently happy on the one simple condition that a certain lost soul on the far-off edge of things should lead a life of lonely torture"

(Le Guin credited James's essay as her starting point, and said she had forgotten Dostoyevsky's earlier version of the same idea when she wrote her story.)
